note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before you work out how much cable a new circuit needs, which information should you collect first?
options: The price of cable at the nearest hardware store
The route length from the drawing, checked on site
The number of electricians who will pull the cable
The make of the breaker already fitted in the panel

questions.stem: A trainee works out that a 1.5 kW heater on 110 V draws 1.36 A. Why should this answer make you stop and check?
options: Heaters are rated in kVA, so watts cannot be used here
Current must always be a bigger number than the voltage
A heater on 110 V will always draw exactly 10 A
A rough check, 1500 ÷ 100, gives about 15 A, not 1.4 A

questions.stem: A heating element has a resistance of 22 Ω and is connected to 220 V. What current flows?
Which is the correct way to rearrange V = I × R to find the resistance?
options: R equals V multiplied by I
R equals I divided by V
R equals V divided by I
R equals V take away I

questions.stem: A 1.1 kW heating element is rated for 110 V. What is its resistance? (R = V² ÷ P)
Which formula gives the power in a resistor when you know only the current and the resistance?
options: P equals I squared times R
P equals I divided by R
P equals R divided by I squared

questions.stem: A 2.5 kW air conditioner runs 8 hours a day for 30 days. Electricity costs J$70 per kWh (a made-up rate for this question). What does the energy cost?
Two 20 Ω resistors in parallel are connected in series with a 15 Ω resistor. What is the total resistance?
Two 60 Ω heating elements are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance?
Why does the total resistance of a circuit fall each time another lamp is added in parallel?
options: Each lamp lowers the supply voltage across the others
The new lamp takes some resistance out of the cable
Each lamp gives the current one more path to flow through
The breaker lets more voltage through as the load grows

questions.stem: Two identical lamps are wired in series across a 220 V supply. What voltage is across each lamp?
A 110 V circuit feeds a 600 W microwave, a 300 W fridge and a 200 W fan, all at the same time. About what total current flows?
A 220 V circuit has a design current of 17 A. The cable chosen is rated 27 A as installed. Which breaker rating suits it best?
A single-phase circuit is 30 m long (one way) and carries 10 A. Each conductor has a resistance of 0.0074 Ω per metre. Counting both the line and the neutral, what is the voltage drop?
The voltage drop on a 220 V circuit works out at 5.5 V. The specification allows no more than 3%. What should you conclude?
options: It fails, because 5.5 V is more than 3 V
It fails, because the drop is 4% of the supply
It passes, because the drop is 2.5% of the supply
It passes, because any drop under 10 V is allowed

questions.stem: Why does a copper conductor's resistance go up when the cable runs hot?
options: Copper resists current more as its temperature rises
Heat makes the copper conductor shorter and thinner
Heat makes the cable's insulation conduct
Hot cables carry less voltage from the supply

questions.stem: If you double the cross-sectional area of a copper conductor and keep its length the same, what happens to its resistance?
A round conductor is 1.78 mm across (its diameter). About what is its cross-sectional area? (Area = π × r², π = 3.142)
An insulation resistance tester reads 2.5 MΩ. How many ohms is this?
A clamp meter shows 350 mA. What is this in amps?
A control transformer has 880 turns on its primary and 440 turns on its secondary. It is fed at 220 V. Ignoring losses, what is the secondary voltage?
A motor takes 2 000 W from the supply and gives out 1 700 W at its shaft. What is its efficiency?
A machine on 220 V draws 8 A and has a power factor of 0.8. What is its true power, in watts?
A straight conduit run is 47 m long. Conduit comes in 3 m lengths, with one coupler at each joint between lengths. How many couplers are needed?
Five cable runs of 33 m are needed, each with 1 m extra for terminating. Cable comes on 100 m drums, and a run may not be joined. How many drums are needed?
A job needs 120 m of cable at J$185 per metre and 14 boxes at J$450 each. What is the material cost before tax?
Cable costs J$18 500 for a 100 m drum, or J$210 a metre cut to length. A job needs 85 m. Which is cheaper, and by how much?
Wiring one house is estimated at 96 worker-hours. A team of 4 electricians works 8 hours a day. How many days should the job take?
A team must finish first-fix wiring in 6 apartments in 9 working days. After 4 days, 2 apartments are done. What should the team leader conclude?
options: The job is ahead, since a third of the work is done
The job is on time, since only four days have passed
The work rate can stay the same and still finish
The job is behind, and the rate must rise to finish

questions.stem: A room is 4 m × 3 m. The lamps put a total of 3 600 lumens onto the working surface. What is the average light level? (lux = lumens ÷ area in m²)
A cable is to run straight from one corner of a ceiling to the opposite corner. The ceiling is 6 m by 8 m. How long is the straight run?
A 12 V, 100 Ah battery feeds an emergency light that draws 4 A. Ignoring losses and the safe depth of discharge, how long could it run in theory?
A cable is rated 32 A at 30 °C. It will run in a roof space at 45 °C, where the table gives a correction factor of 0.79. About what current is it now good for?
A resistor is marked 470 Ω ± 5%. Which measured value is outside its tolerance?
A meter reads 226 V on a supply that a calibrated meter shows as 220 V. What is the first meter's error, as a percentage of the true value?
Four readings of the same conductor's resistance are 0.82, 0.86, 0.79 and 0.85 Ω. What is the mean?
A load calculation gives a design current of 23.4 A. How should you use this figure when choosing a cable from a table?
options: Choose a cable rated at or above 23.4 A; do not round down
Round down to 23 A, since 0.4 A is too small to matter
Round to 20 A, the nearest standard breaker size
Drop the decimal and use the cable rated nearest 23 A

questions.stem: A shop has eight 110 V general outlets. The engineer's design guide says to allow 180 VA for each outlet. What total load is allowed for?
Which formula gives the current drawn by a heater when you know its power and the supply voltage?
options: I equals P multiplied by V
I equals P divided by V
I equals V divided by P
I equals P take away V

questions.stem: Copper's resistivity is often written as 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m. Which number is the same?
A specification limits cables to 40% of a trunking's inside area. The trunking is 50 mm × 50 mm inside. What total cable area is allowed?
A trainee works out that a 100 W lamp on 110 V has a resistance of 1.1 Ω. Which check shows the answer is wrong?
options: Using 1.1 Ω, P = V² ÷ R gives about 11 000 W, not 100 W
Lamps are not rated in watts, so the sum cannot work
Resistance must always be bigger than the supply voltage
A lamp's resistance in ohms equals its rated current

questions.stem: An electrician earns J$1 200 an hour and a helper J$700 an hour. Both work 7 hours. What is the labour cost?
A wiring job's cost is split between materials and labour in the ratio 3 : 2. The total is J$150 000. What is the labour cost?
Why should a Level 3 electrician write the formula and each step of a cable calculation on the job sheet?
options: So the customer can be charged for the extra paperwork
Because the answer is not needed if the steps are shown
So another person can check the working and find any slip
Because calculators are not allowed on a job site

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences and show your working. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A 24 V DC control circuit draws 0.5 A. What power does it use, in watts?
What is the total resistance, in ohms, of a 30 Ω resistor and a 60 Ω resistor connected in parallel?
How many kilowatt-hours does a 1 500 W heater use in 4 hours?
A generator turns at 3 000 rev/min. How many revolutions does it make each second?
What is the voltage drop, in volts, when 5 A flows through a total conductor resistance of 0.8 Ω?
A transformer steps 220 V down to 24 V. Its primary has 1 100 turns. How many turns does its secondary have?
A 3 kW load runs on 220 V. What current does it draw, to the nearest whole amp?
Which law states that the current in a resistor is equal to the voltage across it divided by its resistance?
A circuit carries 18 A and its breaker is rated 20 A. What percentage of the breaker rating is being used?
What power, in watts, is used by a 48 Ω element carrying 5 A?
A transformer gives out 950 W for every 1 000 W it takes in. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?
A load takes 1 760 W of true power and 2 200 VA of apparent power. What is its power factor?
Each socket outlet box needs 2 fixing screws. How many screws are needed for 3 rooms with 6 boxes each, plus 10% spare, rounded up to a whole number?
A 12 V DC supply feeds a 4 Ω resistor and a 2 Ω resistor in series. What current flows, in amps?

essays.stem: A 220 V single-phase pump motor gives 1.5 kW at its shaft. Its efficiency is 80% and its power factor is 0.85. Work out the input power and the running current, and explain why the starting current must be thought about when choosing the protection.
essays.modelAnswer: The shaft output is not the power taken from the supply, because some power is lost as heat and friction. Input power = output ÷ efficiency = 1 500 ÷ 0.8 = 1 875 W. Because the power factor is 0.85, the supply must provide more volt-amperes than watts: apparent power = 1 875 ÷ 0.85 = about 2 206 VA. The running current is apparent power ÷ voltage = 2 206 ÷ 220 = about 10 A. When a motor starts, it draws a current several times bigger than its running current for a short time, until it gets up to speed. If the breaker is chosen only on the running current, it may trip every time the pump starts. So the protection must suit motor starting, for example a breaker with a suitable tripping curve or a motor starter with an overload set to the running current, as the motor and breaker makers' data show. The cable must still be protected, so the choices are checked against the cable's corrected rating.
markingPoints: Input power 1 875 W worked correctly (output ÷ efficiency)
Apparent power about 2 206 VA using the power factor
Running current about 10 A worked correctly
Explains that starting current is several times the running current
Protection suited to motor starting (curve or overload), using makers' data, and cable still protected

essays.stem: A 110 V circuit is 40 m long and carries 12 A. Each conductor has a resistance of 0.0074 Ω per metre. Work out the voltage drop and its percentage of the supply, compare it with a 3% limit, and explain two ways to bring it within the limit.
essays.modelAnswer: Current flows out on the line and back on the neutral, so the length of conductor is 2 × 40 = 80 m. The resistance is 80 × 0.0074 = 0.592 Ω. The voltage drop is 12 × 0.592 = 7.1 V. As a percentage of 110 V this is 7.1 ÷ 110 × 100 = about 6.5%, which is more than twice the 3% limit, so the circuit fails. One fix is a bigger cable: doubling the cross-sectional area roughly halves the resistance and the drop. Another fix is to supply the load at 220 V, if the equipment is rated for it: the same power needs about half the current, so the drop in volts halves and is a smaller share of a bigger voltage. The circuit could also be shortened by moving the panel feed or split into two circuits. I would rework the sum after any change.
markingPoints: Uses twice the route length (80 m) for line and neutral
Voltage drop about 7.1 V worked correctly
Percentage about 6.5%, so it fails the 3% limit
First valid fix explained, for example a larger cable
Second valid fix explained, for example 220 V supply, shorter route or split circuit

essays.stem: Two 100 W, 110 V lamps can be connected to a 110 V supply in series or in parallel. Work out the current and total power in each case, and explain why house wiring connects lamps in parallel.
essays.modelAnswer: Each lamp's resistance is R = V² ÷ P = 110 × 110 ÷ 100 = 121 Ω (ignoring the change with temperature). In parallel, each lamp gets the full 110 V, so each takes 100 W and about 0.91 A. The total current is about 1.82 A and the total power 200 W. In series, the resistances add to 242 Ω. The current is 110 ÷ 242 = about 0.45 A, and the total power is 110 × 0.45 = about 50 W, so each lamp gives only about 25 W and glows dimly, because each gets only 55 V. House wiring uses parallel so that every lamp and appliance gets the full supply voltage it is rated for, each can be switched on its own, and if one lamp fails the others keep working. In series, one failed lamp breaks the circuit for all of them.
markingPoints: Lamp resistance 121 Ω worked out
Parallel: about 0.91 A each, 1.82 A and 200 W in total
Series: 242 Ω, about 0.45 A and about 50 W in total, lamps dim
Parallel gives each load full voltage and separate switching
One failure in series stops all; in parallel the others keep working

essays.stem: A customer wants to replace twenty 60 W lamps with 9 W LED lamps that give about the same light. The lamps are on 10 hours a day. Electricity costs J$65 per kWh (a made-up rate). Work out the saving for a 30-day month, and explain how you would present the result to the customer.
essays.modelAnswer: Each lamp saves 60 − 9 = 51 W. Twenty lamps save 20 × 51 = 1 020 W, which is 1.02 kW. Over 10 hours a day for 30 days this is 1.02 × 10 × 30 = 306 kWh. At J$65 per kWh the saving is 306 × 65 = J$19 890 a month. I would set out the working in a short table: old load, new load, hours, kWh saved and cost saved, so the customer can follow it. I would say that the rate used is an example and that the real saving depends on the tariff on their bill and how long the lamps are really on. I would also give the cost of the new lamps and fitting, and show how many months it takes for the saving to pay for them. The figures should be checked by a second person before the customer sees them.
markingPoints: Saving per lamp 51 W and 1.02 kW in total
306 kWh per month worked correctly
J$19 890 saving worked correctly
Clear table or set-out working for the customer, with assumptions stated
Mentions payback against the cost of new lamps, or checking by another person

essays.stem: Describe how you would work out the cable, conduit, boxes and accessories for a small room from a scaled drawing, and turn the quantities into a priced material list. Use your own small example.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the drawing's scale, for example 1:50, and confirm a known dimension on site. I count each item from the drawing using the symbol key: for example 4 socket outlets, 2 switches and 3 lights, giving 9 boxes. I measure each conduit route on the drawing, multiply by the scale and add the drops to each box height. Say the routes total 22 m: I add about 10% for bends and waste, giving 24.2 m, and divide by the 3 m length to get 8.07, so I order 9 lengths, always rounding up. Cable length is the route length times the number of conductors pulled in, plus extra at each end for terminating. I list every item with its size, quantity, unit price in J$ and line total, add the totals, take off any trade discount, and add GCT at the current rate. Another person checks the list against the drawing before ordering.
markingPoints: Checks the scale and counts items from the symbol key
Measures routes, converts by scale and adds drops
Adds a waste allowance and rounds up to whole lengths or packs
Prices each line in J$, totals, discount and GCT at the current rate
Gives a worked example and has the list checked

essays.stem: Explain how to rearrange P = I² × R to find the current. Use it to find the current in a 2 000 W element with a resistance of 24.2 Ω, and explain how you would check your answer another way.
essays.modelAnswer: To find I, first divide both sides by R, which gives I² = P ÷ R. Then take the square root of both sides, which gives I = √(P ÷ R). For the element, P ÷ R = 2 000 ÷ 24.2 = 82.6, and the square root of 82.6 is about 9.09 A. To check, I can use a different formula. Ohm's law gives the voltage across the element: V = I × R = 9.09 × 24.2 = about 220 V, which matches a normal Jamaican supply. Then P = V × I = 220 × 9.09 = about 2 000 W, which matches the rating. A quick estimate also helps: 2 000 W on about 200 V is about 10 A, so 9.09 A is sensible. If the check had given a strange voltage, I would look again for a slip in the working.
markingPoints: Divides by R to get I² = P ÷ R
Takes the square root: I = √(P ÷ R)
Current about 9.09 A worked correctly
Checks with V = I × R and P = V × I (about 220 V and 2 000 W)
Uses an estimate or says what to do if the check fails

essays.stem: A cable is rated 32 A at 30 °C. On a job it will run in a roof at 40 °C (factor 0.87) and be grouped with other circuits (factor 0.8). Work out its new rating, decide whether a 25 A breaker can protect it, and explain why correction factors are needed.
essays.modelAnswer: Both factors apply together, so they are multiplied: 32 × 0.87 × 0.8 = 22.3 A. This is the most current the cable can carry in these conditions without overheating. A 25 A breaker is bigger than 22.3 A, so the cable could carry an overload above its rating without the breaker tripping. The 25 A breaker is not suitable. Either a 20 A breaker is used, if the design current is 20 A or less, or a larger cable is chosen whose corrected rating is at least 25 A. Correction factors are needed because a cable's rating in the table assumes standard conditions. Hot air around it, or other loaded cables beside it, stop it from losing heat. Too much heat damages the insulation over time and can lead to a fault or a fire.
markingPoints: Multiplies both factors: about 22.3 A
25 A breaker is not suitable because it is above the corrected rating
Gives a correct alternative: 20 A breaker or a larger cable
Explains that table ratings assume standard conditions
Links heat build-up to insulation damage, faults or fire

essays.stem: An apprentice hands you this working for a 2.4 kW, 220 V heater: "I = V ÷ P = 220 ÷ 2.4 = 91.7 A, so use a 100 A breaker." Explain what is wrong, give the correct working, and say how you would help the apprentice avoid this mistake again.
essays.modelAnswer: There are two mistakes. First, the formula is upside down: current is power divided by voltage, I = P ÷ V, not V ÷ P. Second, the units are mixed: the power must be in watts, 2 400 W, not 2.4. The correct working is I = 2 400 ÷ 220 = about 10.9 A. A breaker is then chosen at or above this, for example 16 A, as long as the cable's corrected rating is at least the breaker rating. A 100 A breaker would never protect a small cable and could let it burn. To help the apprentice, I would show the working calmly, not just give the answer. I would teach a quick sense check, such as a heater of a few kilowatts on 220 V draws around 10 A, and ask them to write units at every step and check the answer with P = V × I.
markingPoints: Spots the wrong formula (should be P ÷ V)
Spots the unit mistake (kW not changed to W)
Correct current about 10.9 A and a suitable breaker
Explains the danger of the 100 A breaker
Coaching: sense check, units at each step, check with another formula

essays.stem: You record the supply voltage at a site every hour for 8 hours: 221, 218, 224, 215, 219, 226, 220 and 217 V. Work out the mean and the range, compare them with a tolerance of ±6% on 220 V (given for this question), and say what you would report.
essays.modelAnswer: The readings add up to 1 760 V. The mean is 1 760 ÷ 8 = 220 V. The range is the highest minus the lowest: 226 − 215 = 11 V. The tolerance of ±6% on 220 V is 220 × 0.06 = 13.2 V, so the allowed band is 206.8 V to 233.2 V. Every reading is inside this band, and the mean is right on the nominal 220 V, so the supply was within tolerance for the period. In my report I would give the date, place, the meter used and its calibration date, the times of the readings, the table of results, the mean and range, and the tolerance used. I would say that the supply was within limits, but that 8 hours is a short sample, so a longer recording would be needed if the customer still has problems such as lights dimming.
markingPoints: Mean 220 V worked correctly
Range 11 V worked correctly
Tolerance band 206.8–233.2 V and all readings inside it
Report includes date, meter, readings and conclusion
Notes the limit of a short sample or suggests further recording

essays.stem: A team of 3 electricians takes 5 days to wire 4 apartments. The contractor wants the next block of 12 similar apartments finished in 10 days. Work out how many electricians are needed, state your assumptions, and explain how a team leader would use the figure.
essays.modelAnswer: The first job took 3 × 5 = 15 worker-days for 4 apartments, which is 3.75 worker-days per apartment. Twelve apartments need 12 × 3.75 = 45 worker-days. Spread over 10 days, this needs 45 ÷ 10 = 4.5 electricians, so 5 are needed, because you cannot have half a person and rounding down would make the job late. This assumes the apartments are the same size and design, the new workers work at the same rate, materials arrive on time and there are no access delays. The team leader would use the figure to book labour, plan who works where so people do not get in each other's way, and order materials in time. They would track progress each day against the plan and report early to the contractor if the job starts to fall behind.
markingPoints: 15 worker-days and 3.75 per apartment
45 worker-days for 12 apartments
4.5 rounded up to 5 electricians, with the reason
States assumptions: same rate, similar apartments, materials and access
Uses the figure to plan labour, materials and track progress

practical1.title: Design calculations and a priced material list for a small shop
practical1.brief: As a group, plan the final circuits for a small shop from the drawing the assessor gives you (lights, 110 V outlets, a 220 V water heater and a 220 V air conditioner). Choose a group leader who shares out the work and a checker who checks every sheet. Each member does at least one full calculation: the load and design current for a circuit, the breaker and cable choice from the rating table with correction factors, or the voltage drop on the longest run. Then make a material take-off from the drawing, and measure one marked-out route on the workshop wall with a tape to compare with your drawing figure. Finish with a priced material list in J$ (from the assessor's price list) with GCT shown at the rate the assessor gives. Present your results on a flip-chart sheet. No electrical work is done in this task.
materials: Shop floor plan to scale (for example 1:50), with the loads listed, from the assessor
Cable rating table with correction factors, and resistance per metre for each cable size (given as data)
Price list in J$ (made up for the task) and the GCT rate, from the assessor
Calculators, scale rule, 5 m and 30 m tape measures
Calculation worksheets, flip-chart paper and markers
photos: The group with the drawing, showing who has which job
The completed load schedule with design currents
The breaker, cable and voltage-drop worksheets, signed by the checker
The tape measurement of the marked-out route beside the drawing figure
The finished priced material list with discount and GCT lines
The flip-chart summary presented to the assessor
checklist: Took part in planning and shared out the calculations fairly
Worked out a design current correctly, with formula and units shown
Chose a breaker and cable that meet the rule design current ≤ breaker ≤ corrected cable rating
Worked out a voltage drop and compared it with the limit given
Took quantities off the drawing correctly, added waste and rounded up
Priced the list correctly in J$, with discount and GCT at the given rate
Checked another member's work and corrected any slip found
Explained one result to the assessor in their own words
safety: No circuit or panel is opened or worked on in this task
Keep walkways clear when measuring the route; do not climb on benches
Use a step-up only if the assessor allows it, with a second person holding it
Retract tape measures slowly to avoid cuts to the hands

practical2.title: Energy audit of a classroom with savings and payback
practical2.brief: As a group, carry out an energy audit of a classroom or office at the Centre that the assessor names. Read the rating plate of each appliance and light fitting without opening anything (use the assessor's list for fittings out of reach). Each member records the loads in one part of the room, estimates how many hours each is used each day with the room's users, and works out daily and monthly kWh. Together, work out the monthly cost at the rate the assessor gives, find the three biggest users, and propose at least two savings (for example LED lamps, a timer, or a higher air-conditioner set point). For each saving, work out the monthly saving and the payback time from the prices given. Write a one-page report to the Centre's manager and present it. Every member presents one part.
materials: Audit sheet with columns for item, rating (W), quantity, hours per day, kWh per day and per month
Electricity rate in J$ per kWh and prices for the proposed items (made up for the task, from the assessor)
A list of light-fitting ratings for fittings out of reach (from the assessor)
photos: The rating plate of at least three different appliances
The completed audit sheet for the room
The calculations of monthly kWh and cost
The table of proposed savings with payback times
The group presenting to the assessor
checklist: Read rating plates correctly and recorded watts (or worked them out from volts and amps)
Estimated daily hours sensibly, after asking the room's users
Worked out kWh per day and per month correctly for their part of the room
Worked out the monthly cost at the given rate correctly
Worked out a saving and a payback time correctly
Presented one part of the report clearly
safety: Do not open, move or unplug any equipment; read only what can be seen
Do not climb to read light fittings; use the assessor's list
Ask the room's users before touching anything on their desks
Keep cables and walkways clear while you work
